newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese bay in 1950s poisoning case declared safe.
newsitem.headline: Japanese bay in 1950s poisoning case declared safe.

text.p: A provincial official said on Tuesday it is now safe to eat fish from a bay in central Japan contaminated in a catastrophic case of industrial pollution in the 1950s.

Hundreds of people died and thousands suffered from crippling nerve disorders by eating seafood polluted by poisonous mercury compounds dumped into Minamata Bay by the chemical firm Chisso Corp between 1953 and 1960.
It was Japan's worst ever case of industrial pollution.

Joji Fukushima, governor of Kumamoto prefecture, told a news conference the bay was now free from pollution and he was ready to order the removal of an underwater net which has confined fish within its waters for decades.
"The safety of the fishery products has been confirmed. The bay's environment has improved and the bay is in good shape.
"The possibility of Minamata Disease recurring has been eliminated," Fukushima said, referring to the condition caused by the poisoning that first came to light in 1956.
Minamata Bay is about 900 km (560 miles) southwest of Tokyo.
Fukushima said he hoped the removal of its 2,000 metre- (2,200 yard) long underwater net would be completed by September. It has been in place since 1974.
The Minamata case gained international attention through 1972 photographs of badly deformed children by American photojournalist W.Eugene Smith.
In May 1996 after a decades-long legal battle Minamata victims agreed to accept lump-sum compensation payments from Chisso and the local and state governments.
